lead.en: A city by Lake Titicaca nearly four kilometres up

summary.en: By the mid-first millennium, Tiwanaku, at about 3,800 metres, had become the centre of a state whose influence reached from Peru to northern Chile. Its builders raised the Akapana stepped pyramid and the famous Gate of the Sun, carved from a single block of stone. Raised-field farming yielded harvests even at altitude. Around 1000 the city declined, by various estimates because of a long drought.

lead.en: Judaism's central text after the Bible took shape in Iraq

summary.en: For centuries, generations of sages in the Jewish academies of Sura and Pumbedita, under Sasanian rule, debated and commented on the Mishnah. By tradition, Rav Ashi and Ravina completed the work around 500. The Babylonian Talmud runs to thousands of pages of debate on law, ritual and ethics, and remains the basis of Jewish religious study.

lead.en: Seafarers from Indonesia crossed the whole Indian Ocean

summary.en: Malagasy is most closely related to Ma'anyan of south-eastern Borneo, and the Malagasy people's ancestry comes in roughly equal parts from Southeast Asia and East Africa. Estimates place the Austronesian settlement between the 5th and 8th centuries, though the first human traces on the island may be much older. Madagascar marks the western end of an Austronesian expansion that reached as far as Easter Island.

lead.en: A monk drawing up Easter tables invents our era

summary.en: In 525 the Roman monk Dionysius Exiguus, computing Easter dates, began counting years 'since the Incarnation' instead of from Emperor Diocletian. Europe had no zero then, which is why 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1.

lead.en: Quake and fire destroy a city packed with pilgrims

summary.en: In May 526 an earthquake and the fire that followed destroyed Antioch, one of the Byzantine Empire's greatest cities. It was crowded with pilgrims for Ascension, and chroniclers put the dead at around 250,000.

lead.en: Roman law compiled — the bedrock of Europe's legal systems

summary.en: Byzantine Emperor Justinian I had a commission led by Tribonian codify centuries of Roman law. Rediscovered in Bologna in the late 11th century, the Corpus Juris Civilis became the foundation of civil law across continental Europe.

lead.en: Chariot-racing fans nearly topple Justinian

summary.en: Fans of the rival Blue and Green chariot teams united against the emperor under the cry 'Nika!' ('Conquer!') and burned half the city. Justinian was ready to flee until Empress Theodora talked him out of it; Procopius puts the dead at about 30,000.

lead.en: A dimmed sun opens the coldest decade in 2,000 years

summary.en: Throughout 536 the sun shone dimly, 'like the moon', wrote Procopius; snow fell in summer and crops failed from Europe to China. Tree rings mark it as the start of the coldest decade in 2,000 years, blamed on volcanic eruptions.

lead.en: Justinian builds Christendom's largest church for a millennium

summary.en: Justinian I built in five years a cathedral in Constantinople crowned by a vast dome about 31 m across; for nearly a thousand years it was the largest church in Christendom. After 1453 it became a mosque, in 1934 a museum and in 2020 a mosque again.

author.en: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus

lead.en: Korea's Baekje sends a Buddha statue to the Yamato court

summary.en: King Seong of Baekje in Korea sent a Buddha statue and sutras to the Yamato court — in 538 by some sources, in 552 by the Nihon Shoki. The new faith became a battleground for noble clans: the Soga backed it, the Mononobe opposed it. After the Soga won in 587, Buddhism under Prince Shōtoku became a pillar of the state.

lead.en: The first plague pandemic: Constantinople loses thousands a day

summary.en: The first documented plague pandemic appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and a year later ravaged Constantinople, where thousands died each day. DNA from victims confirmed Yersinia pestis; outbreaks recurred for two centuries.

lead.en: Nubia turns Christian, and stays so for almost a thousand years

summary.en: The missionary Julian, sent by Empress Theodora, baptised the king of the Nubian state of Nobatia. The neighbouring kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia followed. Christian Nubia lasted almost a thousand years; among its legacies are the frescoes of Faras cathedral, rescued before the Aswan Dam reservoir flooded the site.

title.en: Founding of the First Turkic Khaganate

lead.en: A Turkic empire stretches from Manchuria to the Black Sea

summary.en: In 552 Bumin, a chief of the Ashina Turks, whose people worked iron for the Rouran, overthrew his overlords and took the title of khagan. Within two decades his son Muqan and his brother Istämi ruled the steppe from Manchuria to the Black Sea and negotiated the silk trade with Byzantium and Iran. The khaganate soon split into eastern and western halves, but it gave its name to the Turkic peoples.

lead.en: The secret of silk leaves Asia hidden in bamboo canes

summary.en: Byzantium paid dearly for silk and even believed it came from India. Around 552 two monks promised Justinian they would fetch silkworms, and returned from Asia with eggs hidden in their bamboo canes — the start of the empire's own silk industry.

lead.en: A firm that would stay in business for over 1,400 years

summary.en: The carpenter Kongō Shigemitsu was invited from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build the Shitennō-ji temple and founded a building firm. Forty generations of Kongōs ran it, and it stayed independent until 2006 — the world's oldest documented company.

lead.en: China is whole again after three centuries of division

summary.en: Sui armies captured Jiankang, capital of the southern Chen dynasty, reuniting China after nearly three centuries of division. The Sui went on to build the Grand Canal linking the north and south of the country.

lead.en: The first Andean empire, eight centuries before the Inca

summary.en: Around 600, a state centred on Huari brought much of the Peruvian Andes and coast under its control. The Wari built administrative centres to a standard plan and laid roads and terraces, much of which the Inca later inherited. By various estimates the capital housed tens of thousands of people. The state broke up around 1000.

title.en: Joya de Cerén, the 'Pompeii of the Americas'

lead.en: Ash preserved not palaces but the daily life of Maya farmers

summary.en: Around 600 (estimates vary by a few decades) the eruption of the Loma Caldera vent buried a Maya village under several metres of ash. The inhabitants seem to have escaped, as no human remains have been found, but adobe houses, kitchens, pots of food and fields of manioc and maize survived. Found by chance in 1976 and a UNESCO site since 1993, the village shows how ordinary Maya lived.

lead.en: The Sui link the Yellow River and Yangtze to feed the north

summary.en: Emperor Yang of Sui linked a network of canals between the Yellow River and the Yangtze, mobilising millions of labourers. The Grand Canal, the world's longest artificial waterway, carried southern rice to the northern capitals for centuries.

lead.en: The oldest wooden buildings in the world

summary.en: Prince Shōtoku founded the temple in 607. According to the Nihon Shoki it burned after a lightning strike in 670 and was rebuilt soon after; its main hall, at least 1,300 years old, is considered the oldest wooden building on Earth.

title.en: Pakal the Great becomes ruler of Palenque

lead.en: A boy king rules 68 years and makes his city a Maya jewel

summary.en: Twelve-year-old Pakal took the throne of the Maya kingdom centred on Palenque and ruled for 68 years. The city flourished as one of the jewels of the Maya world, and his tomb in the Temple of the Inscriptions is a landmark find of American archaeology.

lead.en: China's golden age of poetry and Silk Road trade begins

summary.en: Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty with its capital at Chang'an, one of the largest cities in the world at the time. The Tang era was a golden age of Chinese poetry, Silk Road trade and cultural influence on Korea and Japan.

lead.en: The first Muslim community forms and the Islamic calendar starts

summary.en: The Prophet Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Yathrib, which became Medina. There the first Muslim community-state took shape, and the year of the Hijra became the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

title.en: Brahmagupta and the rules of zero

lead.en: Zero becomes a number, the root of modern arithmetic

summary.en: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, first set out rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers. The Indian decimal place-value system with zero passed through the Arabs to Europe and underpins modern arithmetic.

lead.en: The runaway monk behind 'Journey to the West'

summary.en: In 629 the monk Xuanzang slipped out of Chang'an against the emperor's ban and travelled through Central Asia to India. He studied at Nalanda, toured almost the whole subcontinent and returned in 645 with 657 Buddhist texts, which he spent the rest of his life translating. His 'Records of the Western Regions' is the key source on 7th-century India, and he became the hero of the novel 'Journey to the West'.

lead.en: The caliphate wrests Syria and Palestine from Byzantium

summary.en: The army of the Arab Caliphate under Khalid ibn al-Walid routed the Byzantines. The victory opened Syria and Palestine to the Arabs; Persia was beaten at al-Qadisiyyah in the same years, and Egypt fell soon after.

title.en: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah and the Arab conquest of Persia

lead.en: The Sasanians fall and Iran enters the Islamic world

summary.en: In 636 (or 637 by other accounts) an Arab army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the Sasanian forces of Rustam at al-Qadisiyyah. The capital Ctesiphon soon fell, the Persians lost their last great battle at Nahavand in 642, and the last shah, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651. Iran joined the caliphate but kept its language and deeply shaped Islamic culture.

lead.en: The pandemic's echo strikes the Arab army in Syria

summary.en: Soon after the Arab conquest of Syria, plague broke out in the Muslim army's camps, an echo of the Justinianic pandemic. Tradition holds that some 25,000 soldiers died, including the commander Abu Ubayda.

lead.en: Fustat seeds Cairo as the Nile valley feeds the caliphate

summary.en: The general Amr ibn al-As took the Byzantine fortress of Babylon and founded the camp of Fustat beside it, the future core of Cairo; Alexandria surrendered in 642. Egypt became the granary of the Caliphate and gradually adopted Arabic and Islam.

lead.en: Christian Nubia halts the Arabs for almost seven centuries

summary.en: In 652 an Arab army besieged Dongola, capital of the Christian kingdom of Makuria, but Nubian archers, nicknamed 'pupil smiters' by the Arabs, beat it back. The two sides agreed the Baqt: Nubia supplied slaves, Egypt supplied grain, wine and cloth. The pact lasted almost 700 years, and Christian Makuria survived until the 14th century.

lead.en: An army camp becomes Islam's first capital in the Maghreb

summary.en: The general Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan as a base for conquering North Africa; its name comes from the word for 'caravan'. It became the capital of the province of Ifriqiya, and its Great Mosque a model for mosques across the Maghreb. Tradition says Uqba later reached the Atlantic and rode his horse into the ocean, lamenting there were no more lands to conquer.

lead.en: A Sumatran sea power controls the Strait of Malacca

summary.en: The maritime empire of Srivijaya, centred on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca and the trade between China and India. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing described it in 671 as a major centre of Buddhist learning.

lead.en: A weapon so secret its recipe was lost forever

summary.en: The incendiary mixture, sprayed from siphons on ships and burning even on water, was used by Byzantium against Arab fleets from the 670s. Its composition was a state secret kept so well that the recipe is lost; most likely it was petroleum mixed with resins.

lead.en: Tang's ally ends up driving the Tang off the peninsula

summary.en: Allied with Tang China, the kingdom of Silla destroyed its rivals, Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668. When the Tang tried to take over the whole peninsula, Silla turned on its former ally and by 676 had driven the Tang armies out. For the first time most of Korea was ruled by a single state, with its capital at Gyeongju.

lead.en: The death of the Prophet's grandson defines Shia memory

summary.en: The army of Umayyad caliph Yazid I massacred the small band of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at Karbala. Husayn's death became a defining event for Shia Islam, deepened the Sunni–Shia split and is mourned every year on Ashura.

title.en: Lady Six Sky arrives at Naranjo

lead.en: A Maya queen who portrayed herself as a warrior king

summary.en: The daughter of the ruler of Dos Pilas came to Naranjo in 682 to found a new dynasty and effectively ruled the city for almost 60 years. Her stelae show her trampling a captive — the pose of a warrior king, unusual for a woman in Maya art.

title.en: Fall of Carthage and the Arab conquest of the Maghreb

lead.en: North Africa becomes part of the Islamic world for good

summary.en: In 698 the Arab general Hassan ibn al-Nu'man took Byzantine Carthage. The fiercest resistance came from the Berbers led by Queen Dihya, whom the Arabs called al-Kahina, 'the prophetess'; she fell around 701. By 709 the whole Maghreb was under the caliphate, and Berber converts formed the core of the army that crossed into Spain in 711.

title.en: The rise of the Kanem Empire

lead.en: A Lake Chad empire whose dynasty ruled for nearly 800 years

summary.en: Around 700 the Kanembu nomads built the Kanem state northeast of Lake Chad, holding the southern end of the caravan route to Libya. In the late 11th century its ruler Hume of the Sayfawa dynasty converted to Islam. The state later shifted to Bornu, and the Sayfawa ruled for nearly eight centuries, until 1846, one of history's longest dynasties.

lead.en: A hotel that has been taking guests for over 1,300 years

summary.en: The hot-spring inn in the Yamanashi mountains was founded in 705, and by family tradition 52 generations of one lineage have run it. Guinness World Records lists it as the oldest hotel still in operation.

lead.en: The Visigoths fall and the story of al-Andalus begins

summary.en: An Arab-Berber army under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed at the rock later named after him and crushed the Visigoths at Guadalete. Within a few years most of Iberia was part of the Umayyad Caliphate, beginning the history of al-Andalus.

lead.en: Byzantine emperors ban icons, starting a century-long fight

summary.en: Emperor Leo III turned against the veneration of icons, and Byzantium split for a century between iconoclasts and icon-venerators. Icons were destroyed and monks persecuted. Veneration was finally restored in 843, which the Orthodox Church still celebrates as the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'.

lead.en: Charles Martel halts the Arab advance into Western Europe

summary.en: Frankish forces under Charles Martel halted the army of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus, between Tours and Poitiers; the governor fell in battle. It marked the limit of Arab advance into Western Europe and boosted the Carolingians.

lead.en: The oldest Turkic texts, carved in runes on stone stelae

summary.en: In 732 and 735 stelae were raised in the Orkhon Valley for Prince Kul Tigin and his brother Bilge Khagan. Their Old Turkic runic texts tell of the campaigns and fortunes of the Second Turkic Khaganate. They are the oldest continuous texts in a Turkic language, deciphered by the Dane Vilhelm Thomsen in 1893.

lead.en: A vassal captures and sacrifices its overlord's king

summary.en: Kʼakʼ Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá, a former vassal of Copán, captured and executed the Copán king Uaxaclajuun Ubʼaah Kʼawiil. Quiriguá became independent and grew rich on trade along the Motagua valley. To mark the victory it raised the tallest Maya stelae; Stela E stands over 10 metres high.

lead.en: The Uyghurs topple the Turks and make Manichaeism a state faith

summary.en: In 744 the Uyghurs destroyed the Second Turkic Khaganate and founded their own state with its capital at Ordu-Baliq. They helped the Tang crush the An Lushan rebellion, and in 762 their khagan adopted Manichaeism, a rare case of it becoming a state religion. In 840 the khaganate fell to the Yenisei Kyrgyz.

lead.en: The caliphate shifts east, toward Baghdad and Persian culture

summary.en: In 747 Abu Muslim raised the black banners of the Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad's uncle, in Khorasan. In January 750 their army defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, on the Great Zab; the Umayyads were massacred, and the survivor Abd al-Rahman fled to Spain. The caliphate's centre shifted east: Baghdad was founded in 762, and Persian influence at court grew sharply.

lead.en: Abbasids beat Tang China and Islam takes hold in Central Asia

summary.en: An Abbasid army defeated Tang Chinese forces by the Talas River in Central Asia. The battle secured Islamic influence in the region, and according to tradition captured Chinese artisans brought the secret of papermaking to Samarkand.

lead.en: A bronze Buddha that consumed a huge share of Japan's copper

summary.en: Emperor Shōmu, shaken by epidemics and revolts, ordered a giant statue of the Buddha Vairocana about 15 metres tall. It consumed a huge share of the country's bronze. In 752 the Indian monk Bodhisena performed the 'eye-opening' ceremony before thousands of guests. The Great Buddha Hall long remained the largest wooden building in the world.

lead.en: A trading post on the Baltic–Volga route, the oldest town of Rus'

summary.en: Tree-ring dating places the oldest buildings of Ladoga on the Volkhov in 753. Scandinavians, Slavs and Finns lived here, and Arab silver and northern furs passed through. According to the Hypatian Chronicle, Ladoga was where Rurik first settled after being invited to rule.

lead.en: A general's revolt breaks the power of the Tang

summary.en: An Lushan, a frontier commander of Sogdian origin, rebelled and took Luoyang and Chang'an; Emperor Xuanzong fled. The war lasted until 763, and the registered population fell from 53 to 17 million through death, flight and collapsing records. The Tang never regained their former strength.

lead.en: An entire temple carved from a single rock, top down

summary.en: Under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (c. 756–773) the craftsmen of Ellora began cutting into a basalt hillside a temple to Shiva representing sacred Mount Kailash. They removed an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock, carving from the top down a courtyard, a multi-storey shrine, life-size elephants and reliefs from the epics. It is one of the largest monolithic structures in the world; Ellora has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

lead.en: The Round City rises as a hub of Islamic learning

summary.en: Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris: the Round City, named Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Baghdad quickly grew into one of the world's largest cities and a centre of Islamic science, trade and culture.

lead.en: The Idrisids build the city that became the heart of Morocco

summary.en: Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet who had fled the Abbasids, founded a settlement on the Fez river, and his son Idris II built a new town on the opposite bank in 808–809. Refugees from Córdoba and Kairouan settled there. The Idrisids created Morocco's first Muslim state, and Fez became its religious and scholarly capital for centuries.

lead.en: Murals that shattered the myth of the peaceful Maya

summary.en: Around 790 three rooms of a temple at Bonampak were painted with scenes of court ceremonies, a fierce battle and the execution of captives. In 1946 Lacandon Maya showed the temple to the American photographer Giles Healey. The murals overturned the then-popular image of the Maya as peaceful priest-astronomers.

lead.en: A plundered monastery shocks Europe and opens the Viking Age

summary.en: Norse seafarers plundered the famous monastery on a tidal island off Northumbria. The raid, which shocked Christian Europe, is traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age.

lead.en: Future Kyoto becomes the imperial seat for a thousand years

summary.en: Emperor Kammu moved Japan's capital to the newly built city of Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto. It remained the imperial seat for over a thousand years and gave its name to the Heian period, the flowering of Japanese court culture.

lead.en: The Pope revives an empire in the West

summary.en: On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's Basilica. The revival of a Western empire sealed the alliance of the papacy with the Franks and sharpened rivalry with Byzantium.

title.en: Drought and the Classic Maya collapse

lead.en: Severe droughts may explain why Tikal and Copán were abandoned

summary.en: In the 9th century the great southern Maya cities, Tikal, Copán and Palenque, were abandoned. Lake sediments and stalagmites show a run of severe droughts then; it is the leading but not the only explanation. Charlemagne ruled in Europe.

lead.en: Java raises the world's largest Buddhist temple

summary.en: Under the Shailendra dynasty, Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple, was raised in central Java. Its terraces carry more than 2,600 relief panels that lead the pilgrim along the path to enlightenment.

lead.en: Jayavarman II proclaims himself god-king, the road to Angkor

summary.en: Jayavarman II proclaimed himself a god-king independent of Java, founding the Khmer Empire. At its height it dominated mainland Southeast Asia, and its capital Angkor became one of the largest cities of the pre-industrial world.

lead.en: A caliph's gift walks over the Alps to Aachen

summary.en: Caliph Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne an Asian elephant named Abul-Abbas. It was shipped to Italy, crossed the Alps in spring and reached Aachen on 20 July 802, living there until 810.

lead.en: A Baghdad scholar gives the world the word 'algorithm'

summary.en: Muhammad al-Khwarizmi, a scholar of Baghdad's House of Wisdom, wrote a treatise on solving equations. The word al-jabr in its title gave us algebra, and the author's name gave us algorithm.

title.en: Venetians spirit away the relics of St Mark

lead.en: The relics were reputedly hidden under pork

summary.en: In 828 two Venetian merchants carried the relics of St Mark out of Alexandria. Tradition says they covered the basket with pork so that Muslim customs officers would not search it. Venice built St Mark's Basilica for the relics, and Mark's lion became its emblem.

lead.en: A witty reply cost Kassia a crown

summary.en: Byzantine emperors sometimes picked a bride at a beauty show, handing a golden apple to the chosen one. Young Theophilos told Kassia: 'Through a woman came the baser things.' She replied: 'And through a woman the better.' Theodora got the apple; Kassia became an abbess and the only known woman whose hymns entered the Byzantine liturgy.

lead.en: The caliph moves his Turkic guard to a new city on the Tigris

summary.en: Caliph al-Mu'tasim, whose Turkic guard clashed with the people of Baghdad, moved his capital to the new city of Samarra further up the Tigris. The Great Mosque with its spiral Malwiya minaret was built there. Samarra remained the caliphs' seat until 892, while the guard took to making and unmaking caliphs.

lead.en: Charlemagne's grandsons sketch future France and Germany

summary.en: Charlemagne's grandsons divided his empire into three: West Francia, East Francia and Lothair's Middle Francia. The partition foreshadowed the later borders of France and Germany.

lead.en: Java's great Hindu temple city, a neighbour of Borobudur

summary.en: Around 850 the rulers of Mataram raised a temple complex on Java dedicated to the Trimurti: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. The central Shiva temple rises 47 metres, and the reliefs of its galleries retell the Ramayana. Prambanan was badly damaged in the 2006 earthquake and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lead.en: The largest adobe city in the Americas

summary.en: Around 850, construction began on Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom, on Peru's arid coast. The mud-brick city spread over about 20 km² and was made up of vast walled palace compounds decorated with reliefs of fish and birds. Around 1470 the Inca conquered Chimor and carried its craftsmen off to Cusco.

lead.en: Hundreds of desert rooms built without wheels or draft animals

summary.en: Around 850, Ancestral Puebloans began building the great house of Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon. Over three centuries it grew to some 600 to 800 rooms on several storeys and remained one of North America's largest buildings until the late 19th century. Roof beams were carried in from dozens of kilometres away, and arrow-straight roads radiated from Chaco.

title.en: The Banu Musa's Book of Ingenious Devices

lead.en: Ninth-century Baghdad automata, programmed by a drum

summary.en: Three scholar brothers of Baghdad's House of Wisdom described about a hundred mechanisms: self-refilling vessels, fountains that changed shape, and an automatic flute player whose tune was set by a pinned rotating drum — often called one of the first programmable machines.

lead.en: Alaskan ash reaches the bogs of Ireland and Germany

summary.en: In the winter of 852/853 an Alaskan volcano spread the White River Ash, later found as far as peat bogs in Ireland and Germany. One hypothesis holds that the disaster pushed ancestors of the Navajo and Apache to migrate far south.

lead.en: The world's oldest working school was founded by a woman

summary.en: In 859 Fatima al-Fihri, daughter of a wealthy merchant from Kairouan, spent her inheritance on a mosque in Fez. A school grew around it and became one of the great centres of learning in the Islamic world, teaching law, grammar, astronomy and medicine. UNESCO and Guinness World Records call al-Qarawiyyin the oldest continuously operating educational institution on Earth.

lead.en: A Rus' fleet suddenly appears before the Byzantine capital

summary.en: Some 200 Rus' boats ravaged the outskirts of Constantinople while the emperor was away with the army. Patriarch Photios described the citizens' terror in his sermons. It is the first reliable appearance of the Rus' in Byzantine sources, two years before the chronicle's 'calling of the Varangians'.

lead.en: By the chronicle, Rurik's rule marks the start of Rus'

summary.en: According to the Primary Chronicle, Slavic and Finnic tribes invited the Varangian Rurik to rule over them. Chronicle tradition dates the beginning of Rus' and of the Rurikid dynasty, which ruled for over seven centuries, to this event.

lead.en: Slavic writing is born: an alphabet and the first books

summary.en: The Byzantine missionary brothers Cyril and Methodius arrived in Great Moravia to preach in the Slavic tongue. The alphabet they devised and the liturgical books they translated laid the foundations of Slavic literacy and literature.

lead.en: China prints the oldest surviving dated book

summary.en: In China a woodblock-printed scroll of the Diamond Sutra was produced — the oldest surviving dated printed book. It was found in 1900 in a sealed cave of the Mogao Grottoes near Dunhuang.

lead.en: A tsunami floods Sendai and returns 1,142 years later

summary.en: In 869 an earthquake off northeastern Japan sent a tsunami kilometres inland across the Sendai plain. The chronicle Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku reports a thousand drowned; the disaster repeated itself 1,142 years later, in 2011.

lead.en: East African slaves hold southern Iraq for 14 years

place.en: Basra and the lower Tigris and Euphrates

summary.en: The Zanj, East African slaves who drained the salt flats of southern Iraq, rose under Ali ibn Muhammad. They built their own capital, al-Mukhtara, and sacked Basra in 871. It took the Abbasids 14 years to crush one of the largest slave revolts in history.

title.en: Abbas ibn Firnas tries to fly

lead.en: A Córdoba polymath flies on wings but forgets a tail

summary.en: According to the 17th-century historian al-Maqqari, the Andalusi inventor covered himself in feathers, fitted wings and flew a considerable distance, but badly hurt his back on landing: he had not realised that birds land on their tails and had not made himself one.

lead.en: Per the chronicle, Novgorod and Kiev unite under one prince

summary.en: According to the Primary Chronicle, Prince Oleg of Novgorod killed Kiev's rulers Askold and Dir and made the city his capital. The union of Novgorod and Kiev is traditionally seen as the founding of the Kievan Rus' state.

title.en: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

lead.en: Árpád's Magyars settle the Danube plain, splitting the Slavs

summary.en: Around 895 the Hungarian tribes led by Árpád crossed the Carpathians and settled the middle Danube plain. Their arrival split the western and southern Slavs and laid the foundation of the Hungarian state.

lead.en: A pope puts his predecessor's corpse on trial

summary.en: Pope Stephen VI had the body of Pope Formosus, dead for nine months, exhumed, propped on a throne and tried, with a deacon answering for him. The corpse was found guilty, its blessing fingers were cut off and it was thrown into the Tiber; within months outraged Romans deposed Stephen himself.

lead.en: Casting so fine that scholars doubted how old it was

summary.en: In 1938 a villager in Igbo-Ukwu, Nigeria, digging a cistern, struck bronze vessels. Excavations showed they were cast in the 9th–10th centuries by the lost-wax method with jewel-like detail, earlier than the famous bronzes of Ife and Benin. Tens of thousands of glass beads, some from far away, were found nearby, evidence of trade across the Sahara or the Indian Ocean.

lead.en: At the equinox a serpent of shadow slides down the pyramid

summary.en: As the Classic Maya cities of the south emptied, Chichen Itza rose in the northern Yucatán. Its pyramid of Kukulcán is famous for the equinox, when shadows on its northern stairway form the body of a serpent. The city had Mesoamerica's largest ballcourt, about 168 metres long, and a sacred cenote into which offerings and victims were cast.

lead.en: The Philippines' oldest document is a debt waiver

summary.en: The text is dated Saka year 822 — AD 900. It releases the children of one Namwaran from a debt of 1 kati and 8 suwarnas of gold (about 865 grams). A labourer found the plate by chance in 1987; it is the earliest dated document known from the Philippines.

lead.en: Ismailis found a caliphate to rival Baghdad

summary.en: The missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i rallied the Kutama Berbers in the mountains of present-day Algeria and in 909 overthrew the Aghlabids, who ruled Ifriqiya for the Abbasids. In January 910 Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi, who claimed descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima, was proclaimed caliph at Raqqada near Kairouan. The Ismaili caliphate challenged Baghdad, conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo.

lead.en: The oldest surviving treaty between Rus' and another power

summary.en: After his campaign against Constantinople, Prince Oleg won a treaty giving Rus' merchants duty-free trade and upkeep in the city. The text survives in the Primary Chronicle and is the oldest record of Rus' law.

title.en: The Khitans found the Liao dynasty

lead.en: The people who gave China the name 'Cathay'

summary.en: Under Abaoji the nomadic Khitans founded in 916 an empire that ruled northern China and Mongolia for over two centuries. Their neighbours in Central Asia and Rus' named the whole country after them — hence the Russian 'Kitai' and medieval Europe's 'Cathay'.

lead.en: A caliph's embassy, and Ibn Fadlan's notes on the Rus'

summary.en: In 922 an embassy from the caliph of Baghdad reached the ruler of Volga Bulgaria, and the country officially adopted Islam. The embassy's secretary, Ibn Fadlan, left notes describing Rus' merchants and a ship burial, one of the most vivid accounts of early Rus'.

title.en: The Qarmatians steal the Black Stone

lead.en: A radical sect raids Mecca during the Hajj

summary.en: The Qarmatians, an Ismaili sect that had built a state in Bahrain, stormed Mecca during the Hajj under Abu Tahir al-Jannabi. They killed thousands of pilgrims and carried the Black Stone away from the Kaaba. It was returned only in 951.

title.en: The first Althing meets at Þingvellir

lead.en: The world's oldest parliament met in the open air

summary.en: In 930 Iceland's Norse settlers began gathering each summer in the Þingvellir valley to make laws and settle disputes, with a lawspeaker reciting the law from memory, a third each year. The Althing met there until 1800, and Iceland's parliament still bears the name.

lead.en: Stakes in a riverbed end a thousand years of Chinese rule

summary.en: Ngô Quyền drove iron-tipped stakes into the bed of the Bạch Đằng, hidden by the high tide, and lured the fleet of the Southern Han there. As the tide ebbed, the ships were impaled and destroyed. The victory ended more than a thousand years of Chinese rule, and Vietnam became independent.

lead.en: Record lava flood witnessed by Iceland's first settlers

summary.en: Around 939 the Eldgjá fissure in southern Iceland poured out more lava than any other eruption in historical times. Viking settlers witnessed it; one hypothesis sees echoes in the poem Völuspá and links it to Iceland's conversion.

title.en: Igor of Kiev killed by the Drevlians

lead.en: A second round of tribute costs the prince his life

summary.en: According to the Primary Chronicle, Prince Igor, having collected tribute from the Drevlians, came back for more and was killed near Iskorosten. His widow Olga took brutal revenge and burned the town, then fixed set amounts of tribute and places for collecting it.

lead.en: The caliph becomes a figurehead under Shia emirs

summary.en: Ahmad ibn Buya from the mountains of Daylam, given the title Mu'izz al-Dawla, took Baghdad. The Abbasid caliph kept his throne and religious authority, but real power in Iraq and Iran passed for a century to the Shia Buyid dynasty, until the Seljuks arrived in 1055.

lead.en: The blast forms Heaven Lake and dusts Japan with ash

summary.en: In late 946 the volcano on today's China–North Korea border produced one of the most powerful eruptions in human history, forming the crater of Heaven Lake. Ash reached Japan, where chronicles recorded the ashfall.

lead.en: Warmth carries the Vikings to Greenland and America

summary.en: From about 950 to 1250 the North Atlantic was noticeably warmer. In these centuries the Norse farmed Greenland and reached America, and vineyards grew in England. The warmth was not globally synchronous; it peaked at different times in different regions.

title.en: Rise of Tollan, capital of the Toltecs

lead.en: The Toltecs become legendary ancestors to the Aztecs

summary.en: Around 950 the city of Tollan (Tula) in central Mexico became the capital of the Toltecs. The warrior columns of its temple and its influence on Chichen Itza made the Toltecs legendary forebears in the eyes of the later Aztecs.

lead.en: An empire whose roads were ocean routes

summary.en: By tradition, around 950 a dynasty of sacred rulers, the Tuʻi Tonga, descended from the sky god Tangaloa, took power in Tonga. In the 12th–15th centuries its influence spread by large double canoes to Samoa, Fiji, Uvea and Niue. From that age remain the stone tombs, or langi, at Muʻa and the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon, a gateway of three multi-ton coral slabs.

lead.en: The model Viking warrior turned out to be a woman

summary.en: The 10th-century grave held a sword, axe, fighting knife, spears, two horses and a gaming set, and since its excavation in 1878 was the textbook male warrior burial. Bone analysis in 2014 and DNA in 2017 showed it was a woman; whether she was a warrior is still debated.

lead.en: The first Christian on the throne of Kiev

summary.en: Olga, ruler of Kiev, visited Constantinople, where Emperor Constantine VII received her with honours and, according to the chronicle, she was baptised. Her son Sviatoslav remained pagan, but three decades later her grandson Vladimir baptised all of Rus'.

lead.en: An age of cities, compasses, gunpowder and paper money begins

summary.en: General Zhao Kuangyin proclaimed himself emperor and founded the Song dynasty with its capital at Kaifeng. The Song era saw booming cities, commerce and technology, from printing and the compass to gunpowder and paper money.

lead.en: Birth of the Holy Roman Empire, which lasts until 1806

summary.en: Otto I, King of Germany and victor over the Magyars at Lechfeld, was crowned emperor by Pope John XII in Rome. The date is regarded as the birth of the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.

lead.en: The first record of the Andromeda Galaxy, a 'small cloud'

summary.en: The Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi checked Ptolemy's star catalogue against his own observations and gave the stars Arabic names, many of which, like Aldebaran, are still used. The book contains the first description of the Andromeda Galaxy, as a 'small cloud', and probably of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

lead.en: A Kievan prince breaks the power that long ruled the steppe

summary.en: Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev defeated the Khazars, took the Don fortress of Sarkel and, according to Arab sources, sacked their capital Atil. The Khazar Khaganate, long the dominant steppe power, soon ceased to exist.

lead.en: The king after whom Bluetooth is named

summary.en: Harald Bluetooth raised the stone for his parents and boasted on it that he had won Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. A thousand years later engineers named a wireless standard after him for its 'uniting' role, and built its logo from the runes of his initials.

lead.en: Mieszko I adopts Latin Christianity and founds Polish statehood

summary.en: Duke Mieszko I of the Piast dynasty was baptised in the Latin rite, probably on 14 April 966. The event is regarded as the birth of the Polish state and drew Poland into Western Christendom.

lead.en: The Fatimids build a capital, soon home to al-Azhar

summary.en: The Fatimid general Jawhar conquered Egypt and founded a new city, al-Qahira, next to Fustat. Cairo became the capital of the Fatimid Caliphate, and the al-Azhar mosque founded soon after grew into a leading centre of Islamic learning.

lead.en: Sviatoslav holds out for three months, then leaves the Danube

summary.en: Prince Sviatoslav, who had conquered Bulgaria, was besieged in Dorostolon by the army and fleet of Emperor John Tzimiskes. After three months of fighting he made peace and agreed to leave the Balkans. On the way home, at the Dnieper rapids, he was killed by the Pechenegs in 972.

lead.en: A Fatimid mosque becomes Sunni Islam's leading university

summary.en: The Fatimids, who had founded Cairo, held the first Friday prayer in their new al-Azhar ('the Radiant') mosque in 972. From 988 it employed salaried scholars. Built to spread Shia teaching, after the Fatimids fell it became the leading university of the Sunni world and has trained theologians and jurists for more than a thousand years.

lead.en: 'Greenland' was named as a sales pitch

summary.en: Exiled from Iceland for killings, Erik spent three years exploring the huge island to the west, then gave it an appealing name on purpose: people, he said, would be keener to go if the land had a good name. Around 985, 25 ships of settlers followed him; 14 arrived.

title.en: Hugh Capet becomes King of France

lead.en: Nobles pick a dynasty that will rule France for centuries

summary.en: After the last Carolingian king of France died, the nobles elected Hugh Capet king. The Capetian dynasty he founded, with its Valois, Bourbon and Orléans branches, ruled France, with interruptions, until 1848.

lead.en: Vladimir ties Rus' to the Orthodox Byzantine world

summary.en: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev adopted Byzantine Christianity and had the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper. The conversion tied Rus' to the Orthodox world of Byzantium and shaped its culture, literacy and statehood for centuries.
